You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

**Verified rule:** For an input grid of height `H` and width `W`, output a grid of height `3H` and width `2W`. Horizontally, each output row is the left-to-right reversal of the corresponding input row followed by the original row. Vertically, use three reflected panels of source rows: bottom-to-top (`rH … r1`), top-to-bottom (`r1 … rH`), then bottom-to-top (`rH … r1`). In zero-based row notation, output row-source order is `H-1,…,0, 0,…,H-1, H-1,…,0`. Within each source row, output `reverse(row) + row`. Preserve all colors; this is a pure reflection/concatenation, not color substitution.

# Continual-ARC pattern notes

## Alternating horizontal marker runs
Evidence from solved task `task-d380c220`:
- The grid had a uniform background (demo: 9; test: 3) with marker cells (demo: 4; test: 0).
- In each row, where marker cells were two columns apart (one cell between them), the gap cell was changed to color 2.
- Existing marker cells and all other cells remained unchanged. This was applied independently per row; no vertical filling.
- Demo showed several horizontal runs of 4 markers with alternating gap cells; test contained shorter runs, including rows with markers at columns 0, 2, and 4. Submitting color 2 in the intervening cells solved the test.

When a future grid resembles this pattern, identify the marker/background colors and fill only single-cell horizontal gaps between same-row markers with 2. Verify no unrelated cells or vertical gaps are changed.

### Additional confirmed recurrence evidence: `task-d380c220` (2026-10-21)
- Demo was 13×21, background 8, marker 0. The output changed every background cell lying between consecutive markers in the same row at a one-cell gap to color 2; e.g. row 3 had markers across alternating columns and the gaps became 2. Markers and all unrelated background cells were preserved. A shorter run with two markers was also bridged; a row with gaps of different lengths showed only single-cell gaps bridged.
- Test was 27×15, background 9, marker 8. Applied the identical rule: for each row independently, change a 9 to 2 exactly when its immediate left and right neighbors are both 8. Keep all 8s and other 9s. The resulting grid was accepted correct with zero wrong submissions.
- Thus the rule generalizes across marker/background colors and grid dimensions; it is local horizontal interpolation only, not a global pattern completion and not vertical filling. A simple check is: output[r][c]=2 iff input[r][c] is background and input[r][c-1]=input[r][c+1]=marker; otherwise preserve the input cell.
